blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A confidence interval (CI) is a range calculated from a sample by a procedure that, over repeated samples, captures the true parameter a stated proportion of the time: the confidence level, conventionally 95%. Its general form is: point estimate ± (critical value × standard error).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: The standard error (recall §6.7) says how far a statistic typically lands from the parameter. A CI turns that into a range: go a set number of standard errors either side of the estimate. The confidence level describes the procedure, not the particular interval you computed.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
Where the formula and the number 1.96 come from, for a mean with known σ:

  1. By the CLT (recall §6.6), x̄ is approximately Normal with mean μ and standard error σ/√n. So Z = (x̄ − μ)/(σ/√n) approximately follows the standard Normal distribution. Its distribution involves no unknown parameter; a quantity like this is called a pivot.
  2. The value that cuts off 2.5% in each tail of the standard Normal is 1.96, because P(Z ≤ 1.96) = 0.975. Hence P(−1.96 ≤ Z ≤ 1.96) = 0.95.
  3. Substitute Z: P(−1.96 ≤ (x̄ − μ)/(σ/√n) ≤ 1.96) = 0.95.
  4. Multiply through by σ/√n and rearrange so that μ stands alone in the middle: P(x̄ − 1.96σ/√n ≤ μ ≤ x̄ + 1.96σ/√n) = 0.95.

The random quantity in step 4 is the interval, whose ends depend on x̄. μ is fixed. The same rearrangement with other cut-offs gives 1.645 for 90% and 2.576 for 99%.

Link to the ±2 SD rule. The empirical rule (recall §5.7.2.2.2) says about 95% of a Normal distribution lies within ±2 SD. The exact figure for ±2 SD is 95.45%. The exact multiplier for 95% is 1.96, which rounds to 2. “Estimate ± 2 SE” is therefore the empirical rule applied to the sampling distribution, and 1.96 is its precise version.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Figure 7.1 draws 20 samples of 30 weights from a population whose mean is known to be 11.81 kg, and builds a 95% interval from each. Nineteen of the 20 intervals contain 11.81 kg; one misses. In real research you see only one interval and cannot tell which kind it is.

blocks.alt: Twenty repeated samples, each with its 95% confidence interval
blocks.caption: Figure 7.1. Twenty samples of 30 drawn from a population with mean 11.81 kg and SD 1.75 kg. Each line is one sample’s 95% t-interval; the red interval misses the true mean. The mean is fixed; the intervals vary.

points.html: Correct interpretation. A 95% CI does not mean “there is a 95% probability that μ lies in this interval”. Once computed, the interval either contains μ or it does not. The 95% is the long-run success rate of the procedure (Figure 7.1).

Width. The interval widens with a higher confidence level (1.96 → 2.576 for 99%), with more variable data (larger s) and with a smaller sample (SE ∝ 1/√n: SE is proportional to 1/√n). §7.3 uses this to plan sample size.

Which critical value. Use the t-distribution (recall §5.7.2.3) whenever σ is estimated by s, whatever the sample size. As n grows, t approaches z (t₂₉ = 2.045; t₁₀₀ = 1.984), so z is a large-sample approximation, not a separate rule.

blocks.html: CI for a Mean

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A confidence interval for a mean is x̄ ± t(n−1) × s/√n, where t(n−1) is the t-value that leaves 2.5% in each tail with n − 1 degrees of freedom.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: When σ is unknown, which is nearly always, replacing it by s adds uncertainty. The pivot becomes (x̄ − μ)/(s/√n), which follows a t-distribution with n − 1 degrees of freedom rather than the standard Normal. Everything else in the derivation of §7.2 is unchanged, with 1.96 replaced by the t-value.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
Today’s 30 children: x̄ = 11.81 kg, s = 1.75 kg.

  1. SE = s/√n = 1.75/√30 = 0.32 kg.
  2. With 29 degrees of freedom, t₂₉ = 2.045.
  3. Margin = 2.045 × 0.32 = 0.65 kg.
  4. 95% CI = 11.81 ± 0.65 = 11.16 to 12.47 kg.
  5. For comparison, the z-approximation gives 11.81 ± 1.96 × 0.32 = 11.81 ± 0.63 = 11.19 to 12.44 kg, about 0.03 kg narrower at each end. Here, where σ is estimated from 30 children, the t-interval is the correct one.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
cl <- read.csv("data/clinic_children.csv")
w  <- cl$weight_kg[cl$seen_today == 1]      # today's 30 children
t.test(w)$conf.int                           # t-based 95% CI (29 df)
# z-based, for comparison
mean(w) + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(0.975) * sd(w) / sqrt(length(w))
[1] 11.15935 12.46732
attr(,"conf.level")
[1] 0.95
[1] 11.18661 12.44005

The first line is the t-interval of step 4 (11.16 to 12.47 kg); t.test uses s and 29 degrees of freedom automatically. The second is the z-approximation of step 5, slightly narrower because 1.96 < 2.045.

points.html: Formula: x̄ ± t(n−1) × s/√n. The t-interval assumes the observations are independent and, for small n, roughly Normal. For larger n the CLT protects it against moderate skew (recall §6.6.1).
A larger sample shrinks s/√n and, through the degrees of freedom, the t-value too.

blocks.html: CI for a Proportion

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: The Wald confidence interval for a proportion is p̂ ± 1.96 × √[p̂(1 − p̂)/n], where p̂ = x/n is the sample proportion.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: A proportion is the mean of 0/1 values (recall §5.7.1.1, Bernoulli), so the CLT applies to it too. The variance of a single 0/1 value is p(1 − p), so the standard error of p̂ is √[p(1 − p)/n], estimated by putting p̂ in place of p. The pivot argument of §7.2 then gives the interval.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
Sixty of 200 surveyed households are CBHI members.

  1. p̂ = 60/200 = 0.30.
  2. SE = √(0.30 × 0.70/200) = √0.00105 = 0.032.
  3. Margin = 1.96 × 0.032 = 0.063.
  4. 95% CI = 0.30 ± 0.063 = 23.6% to 36.4%.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
The full CBHI survey has 150 members among 500 households.

cb <- read.csv("data/cbhi_survey.csv")
x <- sum(cb$cbhi_member); n <- nrow(cb)
p <- x / n
c(p = p, se = sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n))
p + c(-1, 1) * qnorm(0.975) * sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n)   # Wald 95% CI
        p        se 
0.3000000 0.0204939 
[1] 0.2598327 0.3401673

The same 30% with n = 500 instead of 200 gives SE 0.0205 (the 0.021 of §6.2.6) and a CI of 26.0% to 34.0%, narrower by the factor √(200/500) = 0.63. This calculation treats the 500 households as a simple random sample. They were in fact drawn in 20 village clusters, so the true SE is larger: 0.032 (recall §6.2.6: clustering inflates the variance by the factor DEFF; §7.3 uses it).

points.html: The Wald interval performs poorly when n is small or p̂ is near 0 or 1. It can even run below 0% (§7.2.4). One rule of thumb asks for np̂ and n(1 − p̂) both at least 5 before using it. That is a convention, not a guarantee: simple Wald intervals can cover the true value less often than the stated 95% (Newcombe, 1998). The Wilson and exact (Clopper–Pearson) intervals of §7.2.4 avoid these problems.
Every prevalence, coverage or success rate in a report should carry its CI.

blocks.html: CI for a Difference Between Groups

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A confidence interval for a difference between two independent groups is (estimate₁ − estimate₂) ± 1.96 × SE_diff. For two means, SE_diff = √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂). For two proportions, SE_diff = √[p₁(1 − p₁)/n₁ + p₂(1 − p₂)/n₂].

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Research questions usually compare groups. Each group’s estimate has its own sampling error, and the difference inherits both, so the difference is less precise than either estimate alone. The rule is that variances add, standard errors do not: square each group’s SE, add, then take the square root.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
Write the deviations of the two sample means from their targets as a = x̄₁ − μ₁ and b = x̄₂ − μ₂. The deviation of the difference is a − b, and its variance is the average of (a − b)²:

E[(a − b)²] = E[a²] + E[b²] − 2E[ab].

The samples are independent (recall §5.4), so E[ab] = E[a] × E[b] = 0 × 0 = 0. Hence Var(x̄₁ − x̄₂) = SE₁² + SE₂², and SE_diff = √(SE₁² + SE₂²) = √(s₁²/n₁ + s₂²/n₂).

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
Two means (hypothetical). Urban children: n₁ = 40, mean 12 kg, SD 2.0 kg. Rural children: n₂ = 50, mean 11 kg, SD 1.8 kg.

  1. SE₁ = 2.0/√40 = 0.316; SE₂ = 1.8/√50 = 0.255.
  2. SE_diff = √(0.316² + 0.255²) = √(0.100 + 0.065) = √0.165 = 0.406 kg. This is larger than either SE but smaller than their sum, 0.571.
  3. 95% CI = 1 ± 1.96 × 0.406 = 1 ± 0.80 = 0.20 to 1.80 kg.

Had the interval been, say, −0.2 to 2.2 kg, a true difference of zero would have remained compatible with the data.

Two proportions (CBHI survey). CBHI membership is 69/155 = 44.5% among households where the mother has secondary or higher education, and 31/168 = 18.5% where she has none.

  1. Difference = 0.445 − 0.185 = 0.261.
  2. SE_diff = √(0.445 × 0.555/155 + 0.185 × 0.815/168) = √(0.00159 + 0.00090) = 0.050.
  3. 95% CI = 0.261 ± 1.96 × 0.050 = 16.3 to 35.8 percentage points.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
cb <- read.csv("data/cbhi_survey.csv")
tab <- table(cb$maternal_education, cb$cbhi_member)
tab
prop.test(x = tab[c("secondary+", "none"), "1"],
          n = rowSums(tab)[c("secondary+", "none")], correct = FALSE)
               0   1
  none       137  31
  primary    127  50
  secondary+  86  69
...
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.1628515 0.3584235
sample estimates:
   prop 1    prop 2 
0.4451613 0.1845238

The table gives the counts used above (members in column 1). prop 1 and prop 2 are the two proportions, and the CI (0.163 to 0.358) is the hand calculation. The trimmed lines report a test statistic and p-value, which §8.5 explains. As in §7.2.2, this SE ignores clustering by village; §15.2 (analysis of clustered data) shows the correction.

points.html: Null values. For a difference, “no effect” is 0. For a ratio (odds ratio, risk ratio, rate ratio), “no effect” is 1, so check whether the CI includes 1.

Reading an interval that excludes the null. If a 95% CI for a difference excludes 0, the data are incompatible with a zero difference at the 5% level. This is not the probability that the result is “due to chance”. §8.1 (the logic of hypothesis testing) formalises the link.
Paired data. The formula assumes independent groups. For before–after measurements on the same people, analyse the within-person differences as one sample (§9.2.3, the paired t-test).
For small samples of means, replace 1.96 by a t-value; §9.2.2 (the independent-samples t-test) gives the Welch degrees of freedom.

questions.prompt: A colleague says, “There is a 95% probability that the true mean lies in this interval.” Correct the statement.
questions.answer: The true mean is fixed; the computed interval either contains it or does not. The 95% describes the procedure: if sampling and interval construction were repeated many times, about 95% of the intervals would contain the true mean.

questions.prompt: For today’s 30 children (x̄ = 11.81 kg, SE = 0.32 kg, t₂₉ for 99% = 2.756), compute the 99% CI. Is it wider or narrower than the 95% CI, and why?
questions.answer: Margin = 2.756 × 0.32 = 0.88 kg. 99% CI = 11.81 ± 0.88 = 10.93 to 12.69 kg. It is wider than the 95% CI (11.16 to 12.47 kg) because capturing μ more often requires going further into the tails: 2.756 > 2.045.

questions.prompt: Two independent groups of 50 each have SD 2 kg and means differing by 0.8 kg. Compute SE_diff and the 95% CI for the difference. Does it include 0?
questions.answer: SE_diff = √(2²/50 + 2²/50) = √(0.08 + 0.08) = √0.16 = 0.40 kg. 95% CI = 0.8 ± 1.96 × 0.40 = 0.8 ± 0.78 = 0.02 to 1.58 kg. It just excludes 0, so the data are incompatible with a zero difference at the 5% level, though the lower limit shows the true difference could be very small.

blocks.html: Small-Sample and Alternative Intervals: Exact, Wilson, Median and Bootstrap

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: When the Normal approximation behind the Wald interval fails, other intervals are used. For a proportion: the Wilson (score) interval and the Clopper–Pearson (exact) interval, and, when no events are seen, the rule of three. For a median: an order-statistic interval. For almost any statistic: the percentile bootstrap interval.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: The Wald interval places a symmetric band around p̂ using an SE estimated from p̂ itself. Near 0 or 1 that SE is too small and the band can cross 0. The alternatives avoid the shortcut. Wilson inverts the test, asking which values of p would make the observed p̂ unsurprising. Clopper–Pearson uses exact binomial probabilities. The bootstrap builds the sampling distribution by resampling the data you have.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
Wilson. Keep the unknown p inside the SE and ask for which p the observed p̂ lies within 1.96 SEs: (p̂ − p)² ≤ 1.96² p(1 − p)/n. Solving this quadratic in p gives

centre = (x + z²/2)/(n + z²), half-width = [z/(n + z²)] × √[x(n − x)/n + z²/4],

with z = 1.96. The centre is pulled from p̂ towards 0.5, and the limits always stay inside 0 to 1.

Clopper–Pearson. The lower limit is the p at which seeing x or more events has probability 0.025; the upper limit is the p at which seeing x or fewer has probability 0.025. Both use the binomial distribution (recall §5.7.1.2) directly, so no approximation is involved. The interval is conservative: its coverage is at least 95%, and often more.

Rule of three. If 0 events occur in n independent trials, the one-sided 95% upper limit is the p for which (1 − p)ⁿ = 0.05. Then n × ln(1 − p) = ln 0.05 = −3.00, and for small p, ln(1 − p) ≈ −p, so p ≈ 3/n.

Median. Each observation falls below the population median with probability 0.5, so the number of observations below it follows Binomial(n, 0.5). Choose the largest rank r for which P(X ≤ r − 1) ≤ 0.025. The interval from the r-th to the (n + 1 − r)-th ordered value then covers the median with probability at least 95%. No distributional assumption about the data is needed.

Bootstrap. The sampling distribution (recall §6.5) is what you would see if you could draw many samples from the population. The bootstrap uses the sample as a stand-in for the population: draw n values with replacement from the n observations, compute the statistic, repeat 1,000 or more times, and read off the 2.5th and 97.5th centiles of the results (Efron, 1979).

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
Three adverse events following immunisation (AEFI) among 40 infants. An AEFI is any untoward medical event after a vaccination. At one PHC session, 3 of 40 infants had a minor AEFI, and the infants’ outcomes are independent.

  1. p̂ = 3/40 = 0.075; np̂ = 3, below the rule-of-thumb 5.
  2. Wald: SE = √(0.075 × 0.925/40) = 0.042; 0.075 ± 1.96 × 0.042 = −0.7% to 15.7%. The lower limit is impossible.
  3. Wilson: centre = (3 + 1.92)/43.84 = 0.112; half-width = (1.96/43.84) × √(3 × 37/40 + 0.96) = 0.0447 × 1.933 = 0.086. CI = 2.6% to 19.9%.
  4. Clopper–Pearson: 1.6% to 20.4%, a little wider, as expected of an exact method.

No serious AEFI among 150 infants. The rule of three gives an upper 95% limit of 3/150 = 2%. The exact one-sided limit, 1 − 0.05^(1/150), is 1.98%. “None observed” is compatible with a true risk as high as 2 in 100 (Eypasch et al., 1995, after Hanley & Lippman-Hand, 1983).

95% CI for the median weight of today’s 30 children (median 11.7 kg).

  1. For Binomial(30, 0.5), P(X ≤ 9) = 0.021 ≤ 0.025, while P(X ≤ 10) = 0.049. So r = 10 and n + 1 − r = 21.
  2. The 10th and 21st of the sorted weights are 11.0 kg and 12.6 kg. CI = 11.0 to 12.6 kg.
  3. Actual coverage = 1 − 2 × 0.021 = 95.7%.

Bootstrap. 2,000 resamples of the 30 weights give a percentile interval for the median of 11.0 to 12.6 kg (Figure 7.2), the same as the order-statistic interval. The bootstrap SE of the mean from the same approach is 0.31 kg, close to s/√n = 0.32 kg: a check that the resampling reproduces the formula where a formula exists.

blocks.caption: Figure 7.2. Medians of 2,000 bootstrap resamples of today’s 30 weights. The 2.5th and 97.5th centiles (11.0 and 12.6 kg) form the percentile 95% CI. The spikes reflect that a median of 30 values can take only a few distinct values.

blocks.label: In R (optional)
blocks.html:
binom.test(3, 40)$conf.int                   # Clopper-Pearson (exact)
prop.test(3, 40, correct = FALSE)$conf.int   # Wilson score
library(boot)
cl <- read.csv("data/clinic_children.csv")
w  <- cl$weight_kg[cl$seen_today == 1]
set.seed(2026)
b <- boot(w, function(d, i) median(d[i]), R = 2000)
b
boot.ci(b, type = "perc")
[1] 0.01574218 0.20386475
...
[1] 0.02583603 0.19864234
...
Bootstrap Statistics :
    original   bias    std. error
t1*     11.7 0.005625   0.3855275
...
Intervals : 
Level     Percentile     
95%   (11.0, 12.6 )

binom.test returns the exact interval (1.6% to 20.4%). prop.test without continuity correction returns the Wilson interval (2.6% to 19.9%). In the bootstrap output, original is the sample median (11.7 kg) and std. error (0.39 kg) is the SD of the 2,000 resampled medians, the bootstrap estimate of the median’s SE. The percentile interval matches steps 1–2 above. set.seed fixes the random resampling so the result can be reproduced.

points.html: Which interval for a proportion. Newcombe (1998) compared seven methods and recommended the score (Wilson) and tail-area (exact) methods over the simple Wald interval. Report which method you used.
Rule of three. Upper 95% limit ≈ 3/n when 0 of n have the event. Useful for safety claims (“no complications in 60 procedures” still allows up to 5%).
Median CI uses only the ranks, so it suits skewed data such as hospital stay. Its coverage is at least, not exactly, 95%.

Bootstrap needs no formula for the SE, which makes it useful for medians, ratios and model-based quantities (§15.5.2 uses it to validate prediction models). It cannot rescue a biased or tiny sample: with n = 10 the resamples can only recombine 10 values.

questions.prompt: Two of 25 children in an anganwadi test positive for a condition. Compute the Wald 95% CI and state what is wrong with it. Which intervals would you report instead?
questions.answer: p̂ = 2/25 = 0.08. SE = √(0.08 × 0.92/25) = 0.054. Wald CI = 0.08 ± 1.96 × 0.054 = −2.6% to 18.6%. The lower limit is an impossible negative proportion; with np̂ = 2 the Normal approximation fails. Report the Wilson interval (2.2% to 25.0%) or the Clopper–Pearson exact interval (1.0% to 26.0%).

questions.prompt: A surgeon reports “no wound infections in 60 caesarean sections”. Using the rule of three, what infection risk is still compatible with this record?
questions.answer: Upper 95% limit ≈ 3/60 = 0.05. A true infection risk as high as 5% is compatible with zero infections in 60 operations. (Exact one-sided limit: 1 − 0.05^(1/60) = 4.9%.)

questions.prompt: For n = 50, P(X ≤ 17) = 0.016 and P(X ≤ 18) = 0.032 for X ~ Binomial(50, 0.5). Which ordered values form the 95% CI for the median?
questions.answer: Choose r so that P(X ≤ r − 1) ≤ 0.025. P(X ≤ 17) = 0.016 qualifies but P(X ≤ 18) = 0.032 does not, so r − 1 = 17 and r = 18. The upper rank is n + 1 − r = 51 − 18 = 33. The CI runs from the 18th to the 33rd ordered value, with coverage 1 − 2 × 0.016 = 96.7%.
